newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaraguan Sandinistas find trouble with Washington.
newsitem.headline: Nicaraguan Sandinistas find trouble with Washington.

text.p: Attempts by Nicaragua's left-wing Sandinistas to build bridges with their old enemy Washington backfired on Wednesday when the party was forced to withdraw a campaign advertisement after a complaint from the U.S. State Department.

Washington asked the left-wing Sandinista Front to withdraw what it termed an "inaccurate" television spot showing Sandinista leader Daniel Ortega next to U.S. Congressman Bill Richardson, D-New Mexico.

"We are simply doing what we can to see that the campaign does not contain information or lend an appearance that is inaccurate about an American connection with Mr. Ortega," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Tuesday.
Sandinista leaders, who are trying to improve relations with the United States as Nicaragua's Oct. 20 presidential election approaches, quickly agreed.

"The publicity department of the Sandinista Front tried to demonstrate with this spot that we have the best intentions of having an excellent friendship with the United States," top Sandinista official Tomas Borge said in an interview.
At the heart of the issue are relations between the U.S. government and the Sandinistas, who have surged in the polls recently and have a chance of forming the next government.

For the 1996 election campaign, the Sandinistas have carried out an intense campaign to improve relations with the United States and convince voters a Sandinista victory will not mean a return of the 1980s civil war and U.S. economic embargo.

The Sandinistas have abandoned their Marxist roots, accepted free-market economics, opened a party office in a suburb of Miami, Florida, and discarded their party anthem that referred to the United States as "the enemy of all humanity."
While both sides say they will work together if the Sandinistas win, neither side can forget the past.
The Sandinistas, who governed Nicaragua from 1979 to 1990 with Soviet and Cuban backing, fought an eight-year civil war against U.S.-backed Contra rebels that left 25,000 dead.

Earlier Burns had said "he would not use the word democrat to describe Daniel Ortega," and that U.S. officials "have not forgotten the past" -- comments that awakened fears that a Sandinista victory would lead to a deterioration of relations between the countries.
Ortega said it was natural that U.S. officials could not forget the past given what happened, but in the post-Cold War 1990s U.S.-Sandinista relations are different.
Former U.S. President "Ronald Reagan, who made the war against us, is no longer there and U.S. policy with respect to Central American has changed," Ortega said.

Meanwhile, U.S. Ambassador to Nicaragua John Maisto tried to calm the waters, saying his government favours no particular party and will respect the results of the election, provided it is free and fair.
Pre-election polls give right-wing presidential candidate Arnoldo Aleman a 4-8 percent lead over Ortega, far closer than the 15-point gap that separated the two at the end of 1995.
